CO-2026A-HB1010.s: The law increases support and representation for workers age 55 and older in Colorado. Starting in 2027, certain state groups must meet twice a year, collect data, and work together on issues affecting older workers. Starting in 2028, labor and human services must send a yearly report to lawmakers, and some state boards must include at least one member age 55 or older with knowledge of these issues.

CO-2026A-HB1015.s: Colorado extended the homeless contribution tax credit, which lets taxpayers claim a state income tax credit for donations that help people who are homeless. The credit can now be claimed through state income tax year 2030 instead of ending in 2026. It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1028.s: The law changes the rules for a high school biliteracy diploma note and adds a new diploma note for bilingualism. Students can get these through another local school provider or a state college if their own district does not offer the program, and the student’s district must pay any fee charged for the program.

CO-2026A-HB1029.s: The law expands Colorado’s higher education commission from 11 to 13 members by adding 2 nonvoting student members. One student must come from a graduate research university or 4-year school, and one from a community college, local district college, or area technical college. The governor must make the first student appointments by July 1, 2027, and the student members serve 2-year terms.

CO-2026A-HB1033.s: The law expands Colorado’s cottage foods rules to allow some homemade foods that need refrigeration and some foods with meat. People who sell these foods must take a food safety course, register with the state, and follow limits on the kinds and number of food products they sell. It also raises the yearly sales cap to $150,000, lets health agencies fine some violations, and sets aside money to carry out the law.

CO-2026A-HB1052.s: Passed into law, this measure changes Colorado’s Victim Rights Act for certain victims. It says a defendant or accused person in the same case cannot be the victim’s legal stand-in if the victim is a child or at-risk adult. It also gives victims new rights to be told about certain crime lab notices and hearings, ask to use a preferred name in hearings, and speak at a restitution hearing, where money paid back to the victim is discussed.

CO-2026A-HB1053.s: Colorado changed some motor vehicle office rules and set a backup plan for licensing services. Starting January 1, 2028, owners may transfer license plates to a new vehicle instead of having them retired and reissued in some cases. The state also must keep a plan to help vehicle licensing stay running during disruptions, and $18,170 was set aside for that work.

CO-2026A-HB1063.s: The law requires Colorado’s health care policy department and behavioral health administration to post an easy-to-find list of secure transportation providers on each agency’s website. The list must include providers that have contracts with managed care groups and behavioral health service groups, as needed.

CO-2026A-HB1109.s: Colorado law lets a state board, working with the deaf and hard of hearing office, hire an outside researcher by July 1, 2027 to study sign language interpreting services in the state. If the study is done, the researcher must look at interviews, data, and other states and then report the findings and suggestions by July 1, 2028. It affects the deaf, hard of hearing, and deafblind community and the agencies that serve them.

CO-2026A-HB1116.s: The law changes the time for a facility to try to follow up with a person after an emergency mental health hold, from 48 hours to 72 hours after discharge, not counting weekends and holidays. It also says the state can only license or renew a behavioral health facility if it has a fire safety compliance certificate, with exceptions for telehealth-only providers and some outpatient-only providers. These changes affect people discharged from emergency mental health holds and businesses that provide behavioral health services.

CO-2026A-HB1138.s: Colorado created a new advisory board in the state public safety office to set grant rules, review applications, track data on organized retail theft and gift card fraud, and make policy ideas. The law also creates grants for state, local, and tribal law enforcement and prosecutors to investigate and prosecute these crimes, improve data tools, train staff, and fund prevention efforts. It extends an older crime prevention grant program through November 1, 2029, and requires yearly reporting starting in January 2028.

CO-2026A-HB1143.s: The law lets people use a taxpayer ID number instead of a Social Security number for some background checks tied to school or training programs that are not jobs. For certain programs that work with vulnerable people, a hospital, school, college, or district college must accept either a taxpayer ID number or a fingerprint-based background check. It also lets some applicants get fingerprints taken by local police or another approved place, and it sets civil fines for violations.

CO-2026A-HB1147.s: The law requires Colorado health officials to set up a statewide database with information on certain residential support settings and the agencies that run them. Service provider agencies must send in the needed information starting July 1, 2026, and every three months after that, and the database must be updated within one month after the state gets it. It also says these homes must be treated like other residential properties under local rules such as zoning, fire safety, sanitation, and building codes, and limits extra local rules that do not apply to other homes. The law includes $20,000 from the state general fund and expected federal funds of $60,000 to carry it out.

CO-2026A-HB1187.s: Colorado changed the state fire suppression programs run by the division of fire prevention and control. The law keeps those programs going until September 1, 2037, and updates some wording to use gender-neutral terms.

CO-2026A-HB1193.s: School districts in Colorado must now test the vision of pre-kindergarten students, along with students in kindergarten and grades 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9. The law also changes the wording in state rules from "sight" to "vision." It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1194.s: The law renames the Colorado Professional Boxing Safety Act as the Colorado Combative Sports Safety Act and updates related words to match the new name. It continues the combative sports office and commission until 2037, and lets the two physician members of the commission vote if they have training or experience in emergency, sports, or combative sports medicine. It also lets the office collect safety data, sets rules for which combative sports the law covers, and adds some discipline rules for licensees, promoters, matchmakers, and managers.

CO-2026A-HB1196.s: Landlords must follow court rules to protect and hide personal identifying information in eviction court papers, and they must also hide that information in supporting documents filed with the court. Rental applications must include a notice about what tenant information the landlord may try to check, a plain list of the main things used to review an application, such as credit, rental history, income, and criminal background if used, and whether a third-party screening service is used and its name. The measure became law in Colorado in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1202.s: The law requires the state Department of Local Affairs to present a plan in January 2027 for a statewide strategy on homelessness prevention and resolution. It also creates a new local special district that nearby governments can use to work together on homelessness, including a possible sales tax if voters approve it. Counties may also set aside part of certain document filing fees for affordable housing that serves people experiencing homelessness.

CO-2026A-HB1207.s: Starting July 1, 2027, private businesses in Colorado with 100 or more workers must send demographic workforce data from the federal EEO-1 form in periodic reports to the secretary of state. They must do this even if the federal government stops requiring that report.

CO-2026A-HB1210.s: Would bar the use of certain data-driven pricing and wage tools that rely on surveillance data about consumers or workers when that data is a key factor in setting prices or wages. It would affect businesses that set individualized prices or pay and would give workers ways to see, correct, or challenge data used about them. It would also treat a violation as a deceptive trade practice under Colorado consumer law.

CO-2026A-HB1213.s: The law repeals Colorado’s biomass utilization grant program, which gave grants for biomass use projects. It applies to the state program and takes effect as part of the enacted law. It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1223.s: The law creates a new refundable tax credit for people with children, based on the children’s ages and the taxpayer’s income, and it is meant to match the revenue from ending a software sales tax break. Starting January 1, 2027, downloaded software that can be sold and licensed again will be taxed, with some software still exempt if it is covered by a special license or made for one user. It also changes sales tax rules for some food and drink sellers and adjusts how some sales tax money is split between state funds.

CO-2026A-HB1226.s: Colorado law requires the state air agency to write rules by July 2029 setting limits on nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide emissions from certain electric generating units owned or run by electric utilities. Affected units must meet the limits as soon as practical after December 31, 2034, and owners or operators must send quarterly emission reports. The law also adds reporting for some utilities when a federal order keeps a plant running, and it applies to some utility planning decisions and cost recovery steps.

CO-2026A-HB1233.s: For nonresidential property, the law makes it a petty offense to give false or fraudulent information to the assessor about property value, starting with tax years on or after January 1, 2027. It also lets county attorneys handle cases under this law in county court and can block a property owner from getting interest on a tax refund if a court finds a violation. The law also changes appeal rules by requiring property-specific information and letting counties ask for district court review, while letting the petitioner choose between the board of assessment appeals and district court.

CO-2026A-HB1235.s: Colorado changed several Medicaid rules. The law adds new reporting on nonemergency medical rides, requires notice before some payment cuts for outpatient therapy, and updates the term "qualified alien" to "qualified noncitizen." It also sets rules for jail-based medication treatment payments, asks for data on certain care costs, and ends the state medical assistance and services advisory council.

CO-2026A-HB1236.s: The bill would limit some fees in arbitration agreements for workers and consumers, so they could not be made to pay much more than the cost to file a case in court, unless federal law overrides it. It would also bar an arbitrator who has a rule or pattern of conduct that blocks a person from bringing or arguing a claim in arbitration, and it would require a party to follow award record rules within 120 days or face extra damages. The bill would also remove the current ban on exemplary damages, which are extra damages meant to punish bad conduct, in arbitration cases.

CO-2026A-HB1250.s: The law changes the rules for civil asset forfeiture and nuisance abatement cases in Colorado. It says criminal charges must be filed first before a forfeiture case can move ahead, and it gives people who cannot afford a lawyer a right to defense counsel in these cases. It also creates a fund to pay for that lawyer help and changes how money from forfeited property is split among local government, behavioral health services, and the fund.

CO-2026A-HB1256.s: Colorado law now requires the Department of Corrections to give a person leaving custody at least $100, with no deductions, and to help eligible people get a state ID card unless they choose not to take part. It also ends the old rule that gave a person a ticket to leave before discharge. Starting in 2027, the department must report each year on release money and ID card records, including how many people got these items and the costs involved.

CO-2026A-HB1262.s: The law lets licensed people make certain drugs or devices in Colorado when they follow state and federal rules. It also lets licensed pharmacies and FDA-registered outsourcing facilities supply these compounded items to health care providers, pharmacies, facilities, and organizations, and lets them obtain, dispense, or give them to patients. It bars the state pharmacy board from making rules for these outsourcing facilities that are stricter than state or federal law.

CO-2026A-HB1272.s: The law requires Colorado labor officials to start collecting data on heat and cold related injuries, illnesses, and emergencies at worksites. It also sets up a public web page for reporting these events and lets the state use related data from health and workers' compensation agencies. By July 1, 2028, the state must post a model plan that employers can use to help prevent temperature-related harm, and it gets updated at least every 5 years. The bill includes $76,651 in general fund money for this work.

CO-2026A-HB1274.s: The law lets state agencies give advance grant payments to some nonprofit groups that get state money, instead of paying only after costs are spent. Agencies must set up an approved process, share the option in grant notices, keep the amount as small as possible, and use a risk check that limits advance payments to low-risk groups. Groups that get advance money must show a budget, a spending plan, reports, and return any unused funds.

CO-2026A-HB1276.s: The law changes rules for Colorado courts’ e-filing system so users do not have to promise they will not share personal information with federal immigration enforcement. It also expands state health agency checks of facilities that hold noncitizens in civil immigration cases, sets health and safety rules, and can fine facilities that refuse inspections or do not comply. It also requires training for peace officers on immigration detainers and a public policy on protecting personal information, and it became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1283.s: The law says an employer, or someone working for the employer, generally cannot demand, take, keep, or require an employee, job applicant, or other worker to give up a government ID card. It also makes it a crime to knowingly break this rule, and a harsher crime if someone does it to intimidate or harass a person because of race, color, religion, ancestry, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, or transgender identity, or if they give or threaten to give the ID card to federal immigration authorities. The law took effect as passed and affects employers and people seeking or doing work, including migrant and seasonal workers.

CO-2026A-HB1289.s: The law changes several state tax rules and credits. It requires money to be moved from the general fund to the state highway fund, limits some local use taxes on rail-related building materials, and changes income tax rules for some people and businesses starting in 2027. It also raises some vehicle tax credits and changes some wildfire and energy tax credits.

CO-2026A-HB1298.s: The law gives county and state human services agencies the power to run fingerprint-based criminal background checks for people who care for youth in child welfare cases, following FBI rules. It affects people who provide out-of-home care for those youth. For 2026-27, the state expects $350,000 in federal funds for the department, and $350,000 is set aside for the governor’s office to help carry it out.

CO-2026A-HB1302.s: Colorado’s Bureau of Investigation can set its own operating hours for firearm background checks, as long as it still accepts requests every day except Thanksgiving and Christmas and puts them into the processing line right away. The bureau must also send a yearly report to two legislature committees on check times, hours, outages, and steps taken to work faster. It became law.

CO-2026A-HB1304.s: History Colorado may sell certain mineral rights and royalty interests tied to some properties in Weld County and West Virginia. The state controller must approve the deal before it closes, and History Colorado must give an update to a legislative committee. Money from the sale goes to the state museum cash fund for capital improvements, including work on the collections care facility and other upkeep.

CO-2026A-HB1312.s: Colorado changed how the peace officers standards and training board is set up and what it can do. It adds and removes certain kinds of board members, bars people with revoked P.O.S.T. certification from serving, and limits approval of some instructors and training academies after September 1, 2026. It also says a person must be at least 21 to be a certified peace officer and requires a training update proposal by December 31, 2030.

CO-2026A-HB1324.s: The law makes changes to how the state Division of Professions and Occupations works after a sunset review. It lets some regulators hand off certain admin tasks, gives license holders 25 days to ask for a hearing after a letter of admonition, and allows email notices to license holders. It also renames a $1 renewal payment as an additional fee and restores some rules for architect, engineer, and land surveyor licensing and endorsements.

CO-2026A-HB1328.s: The law changes how Colorado Medicaid nonemergency medical rides are set up and watched over. It requires new advisory board input, more broker and provider rules, driver and vehicle checks, and steps to help schedule rides, including same-day and next-day requests when possible. It also changes how these services are paid for and cuts state funding by $76,639 from the general fund and $20,941,853 from the hospital provider fee cash fund.

CO-2026A-HB1331.s: The law changes how Colorado legislative interim committees work during the 2026 interim. It limits how many bill drafts some interim committees can ask for or send forward, blocks per diem and travel pay for members at those meetings, and stops or pauses several committee meetings, trips, and reports. It also ends two review committees and lowers state spending for the legislative department.

CO-2026A-HB1341.s: The law changes when the Colorado Agricultural Development Authority must give up any unused share of its tax-free bond limit each year, moving the date from September 15 to November 15. This affects the authority and the state system that assigns these bond amounts. It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1343.s: The law lets a state agency send hearing notices and decisions by email or other electronic means if the person asks for it or agrees in writing. It applies to people who must be notified in an agency hearing, including final decisions and first decisions by an administrative law judge or hearing officer. It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1345.s: The law changes how Colorado pays public colleges and universities, starting with the 2027-28 state fiscal year. It renames "performance funding" to "results-informed funding" and changes the terms and measures used to figure that money. For the 2026-27 state fiscal year, it also bars the higher education commission from giving money to nonpublic, private, or proprietary schools for students in financial aid or work-study programs.

CO-2026A-HB1363.s: Colorado lowered the state general fund reserve from 15% to 13% for fiscal years 2025-26 and 2026-27. The reserve then goes back to 15% in 2027-28 and later. This affects the amount the state must keep on hand in its general fund.

CO-2026A-HB1380.s: The law ends the office of the judicial discipline ombudsman on July 1, 2027. That office had served as a private, independent advisor on judicial discipline rules and workplace culture.

CO-2026A-HB1382.s: This law changes how Colorado funds services for people with disabilities and moves some duties to a new state authority. It sets new fees for retired-style license plates starting October 1, 2026, creates a board to award grants and contracts for disability-related programs, and shifts the sale of unique vehicle registration numbers to the Colorado disability opportunity office. It also ends the current disability funding committee on July 1, 2027, and sets reporting and funding rules for the new authority.

CO-2026A-HB1409.s: Colorado changed how state marijuana sales tax money is split up. Starting July 1, 2026, it ends the share that goes to local governments and sends the money to the marijuana tax cash fund, the state public school fund, the marijuana cash fund, and the general fund. It also sets a yearly transfer from the marijuana tax cash fund to the state public school fund on June 30, starting in 2027.

CO-2026A-HB1411.s: The law changes health coverage for some pregnant women and children in Colorado’s medical assistance programs. It adds a $1,100 yearly cap for dental care starting July 1, 2026, and starting January 1, 2027, it limits some behavioral health care to fee-for-service, ends some accountable care and managed care coverage, and bars certain other long-term and home care services for some children unless they were already getting them. It also sets a 25,000-child enrollment cap in the state medical assistance program under certain conditions, ends a required outreach plan, repeals the state children’s basic health plan, and includes a $3,378,166 appropriation with possible cuts of $14,202,723.

CO-2026A-HB1412.s: The law lets Colorado health officials use sample-based methods to find and recover Medicaid overpayments from some providers of nonemergency medical rides and pediatric behavioral therapy. It also lets the state auditor use the same method in some later audits, and requires quick written notice and review of how the overpayment was found. The law changes funding for Medicaid services by cutting one general fund amount by $6,861,775 and raising a cash fund amount by $13,723,550.

CO-2026A-HB1414.s: The law sets a $400 cap on what a health care provider or facility may charge for certain large medical record requests made by a patient’s lawyer or a lawyer for the patient’s personal representative. It also says records must be sent in electronic form when requested and available, and that an invoice must be sent within 30 days before the records are released. If the records are not sent on time or a 30-day delay notice is not given, the records must be provided at no cost, and the $400 cap will be adjusted for inflation starting January 1, 2028.

CO-2026A-HB1416.s: On June 30, 2026, the state treasurer must move $1.2 million from the universal high school scholarship cash fund to the Colorado economic development fund and $2.3 million from that same fund to the general fund. It affects the state funds named in the bill.

CO-2026A-HB1419.s: The law changes how Colorado handles a state tax refund that is bigger than the amount owed under the state spending cap. It directs state offices to figure out the 2024-25 over-refund after a 2026 check on state revenues, and then limit how much of that amount can reduce future refunds in any one year starting in 2026-27. It also sets aside $18,021 from the general fund for the state auditor’s office to carry out the law.

CO-2026A-HB1422.s: The law adds new safety steps for the legislature, the courts, the governor, and some elected officials and candidates. It creates a legislative safety administrator, changes the title of certain house security officers to sergeants at arms, and gives the state patrol more role in the state capitol complex and the governor’s mansion. It also makes some campaign filing and disclosure address rules clearer and lets the public view candidate disclosure statements online.

CO-2026A-HB1423.s: Starting in state fiscal year 2027-28, the department of public safety must ask for money for community corrections each year. Its budget request must include data and analysis about bed space, payment rates for each bed type, and other details about funding needs. The department must also share this information at its yearly SMART Act hearing.

CO-2026A-HB1424.s: Colorado passed a law that sets new safety and consumer rules for ride-hailing companies and their drivers. It requires more background checks, faster review of complaints, and a process for driver suspension or removal, with more rules for large companies. It also adds options for ride audio and video recording, limits some contract waivers, and requires yearly safety and discrimination data reports.

CO-2026A-HB1425.s: The law creates a state board to license behavior analysts and assistant behavior analysts, and people will need a license to practice applied behavior analysis starting July 1, 2028. It also sets rules for licensing, discipline, and who is exempt, and it can punish unlicensed practice as a misdemeanor. The law requires Medicaid payment rules for some applied behavior analysis services, and it sets standards for applied behavior analysis clinics and some day treatment facilities.

CO-2026A-HB1426.s: The law updates several parts of the Colorado Department of Law’s powers and duties based on its 2026 legislative report. It would change rules on data sharing with other state agencies, consumer protection, subpoenas, review of agency rules, and some real estate and medical debt topics. It became law on June 2, 2026.

CO-2026A-HB1427.s: The law updates Colorado’s pre-merger notice rules for big company deals. It changes when companies must file a federal Hart-Scott-Rodino form with the Colorado attorney general, requires a secure way to store the papers, and sets rules for keeping or destroying them. It also gives a 3-day chance to fix a filing problem before civil penalties can be imposed.

CO-2026A-HB1429.s: The law changes how Colorado county human and social services offices handle public assistance programs. It sets up a single county office to lead fraud checks for Medicaid, food aid, child care aid, cash aid, and other benefits, and it creates a fund for money recovered from fraud cases. It also sets timelines for shared county contracts, public data reports, and a new way to organize benefit work across counties.

CO-2026A-HB1431.s: Colorado now lets a person who is licensed, certified, registered, or enrolled in good standing in another country apply for the same kind of license in Colorado, if they meet the state’s rules. The change also covers people with that standing from other states, U.S. territories, or the federal government. It became law in 2026.

CO-2026A-HJR1028.s: This resolution says Colorado should work toward full and fair funding for public schools. It tells lawmakers to review the school funding studies, choose a method to follow, and make a multi-year plan to phase in changes, including possible revenue triggers. The text says one study suggested a base of $12,346 per student and notes the state spent $2 million on the studies.

CO-2026A-HR1007.s: The resolution honors Colorado’s 150th anniversary and the generations of people who helped build the state. It calls on Colorado residents to mark the milestone with gratitude and renewed support for freedom, civic duty, and the state’s history. It also says the state should keep protecting natural resources, support civic education, and strengthen infrastructure for future emergencies.

CO-2026A-SB113.s: Colorado now requires recovery residences to get a license from the Behavioral Health Administration starting July 1, 2027. The law sets rules for how to apply and for basic operating standards. It also requires these homes to report certain serious events, such as a resident death or injury, abuse or neglect, theft of a resident’s property, or drug diversion, and the licensing program is set for later review before it ends in 2033.

CO-2026A-SB116.s: The law ends a reduced property tax value for qualified senior primary homes starting with tax years on or after January 1, 2027. It also changes related county and state reporting rules so they end at the same time. For business personal property, it sets the state tax exemption at $58,000 starting on or after January 1, 2027, and keeps the reimbursement for local tax losses at the 2026 amount.

CO-2026A-SB146.s: Starting on January 1, 2027, retail food stores and third-party food delivery services would have to give out single-use food service items only if a customer asks for them or says yes after being asked. They could give only the items requested, not a bundled package with more than one kind of item. The state health department would also have to post a web page explaining these rules and how they are enforced.

CO-2026A-SB15.s: The law changes the name and wording of several child prostitution crimes to use the term "commercial sexual activity with a child." It also changes some penalties, including required prison terms for certain offenses, a 364-day county jail term if probation is given for soliciting a child, and a class 3 felony penalty for some internet luring cases tied to planned sexual activity. It also removes the spousal exception from the crime of engaging in commercial sexual activity with a child.

CO-2026A-SB155.s: The law creates a state-run enterprise to charge certain home insurers a yearly fee and use that money for grants and other services tied to homeowner’s insurance. It affects insurers that sell multiperil homeowner’s policies in Colorado, and it can help homeowners pay to retrofit roofs to better handle hail and wind, with at least 85% of fee money going to those grants. Starting in 2027, the fee is set at 0.5% of the prior year’s premium, and insurers cannot pass that fee on to policyholders.

CO-2026A-SB156.s: Colorado changed how the state work force development council does its work. The law updates its report, gives it more flexibility to set career path rules based on data and feedback, and updates the duties of the postsecondary and workforce readiness statewide coordinator. It also lowers state general fund spending for the Department of Labor and Employment by $46,605 in fiscal year 2026-27, unless the council gets less money or none at all.

CO-2026A-SB167.s: Starting January 1, 2028, health insurers in Colorado would have to count some out-of-pocket costs for prescription drugs bought directly from a pharmacy or direct-to-consumer site toward a person’s plan limit. People would need to send proof of payment within 90 days, and the insurer could ask for more records if needed. The credit would not apply in some cases, including when the drug cost is higher than it would have been at an in-network pharmacy, when no proof is given, or when the drug is not covered unless an exception is granted.

CO-2026A-SB169.s: The bill makes cleanup changes to several Colorado state laws by fixing old, unclear, or unusable language. It says these changes are not meant to change what the laws mean, and it became law.

CO-2026A-SB174.s: The law says buying or selling legal leads, or paying someone else to find potential legal clients, can be treated as a deceptive trade practice in Colorado. It limits legal marketing to people allowed to practice law in Colorado, people working for them who clearly name them, and nonprofit legal groups. People who break the rules can face civil and criminal penalties.

CO-2026A-SB178.s: The law changes how Colorado funds and runs some health insurance affordability programs. It lets the health insurance affordability enterprise issue up to $100 million in revenue bonds starting on or after January 1, 2027, changes how money is spent and invested, and shifts a tax credit from exchange donations to enterprise donations. It also changes premium help and reinsurance rules, requires more reports and a study, and moves $40 million from the marijuana tax cash fund to the health insurance affordability cash fund.

CO-2026A-SB181.s: Colorado changed rules for the Colorado Works cash aid program. Counties may, rather than must, give some people more time beyond the 60-month limit, and the law narrows who can qualify on that basis. It also pauses the yearly cost of living increase for basic cash aid during the 2026-27 and 2027-28 state fiscal years and removes required reserve money levels and related refill rules for two program reserve funds.

CO-2026A-SB184.s: The bill would expand the list of cancers covered under Colorado workers' compensation for firefighters. It would also make it harder for an employer or insurer to say the cancer was not work-related, by requiring clear and convincing evidence. Firefighters who work for the state would not be covered by this change.

CO-2026A-SB188.s: The bill requires the state health care agency to set up a steering committee by July 1, 2026, to help move certain residential treatment services into the managed care system. It covers services in qualified residential treatment programs and psychiatric residential treatment facilities for people in county human or social services custody. The agency must make a plan by April 1, 2027, start the change by July 1, 2027, and send quarterly reports to lawmakers.

CO-2026A-SB193.s: The law says Colorado is not counted as an employer under local minimum wage rules when the state has a union contract on wages. It also says the state is not a business place that can be taxed by city or town rules on occupations and business places. State budget staff must send lawmakers a request about state worker pay for the 2026-27 budget year by January 4, 2027.

CO-2026A-SB2.s: The law requires investor-owned utilities to offer a payment plan for income-qualified residential customers to help with utility bills. For eligible customers, the monthly bill is capped at a set share of household income, and the gap is covered by credits; it also gives credits to help clear older debt before enrollment. It also adds a charge on customer bills to fund the program and gives some appliance and funding deadline changes.

CO-2026A-SB51.s: Colorado law now requires some app store and device software providers to let an account holder enter a user’s birth date, age, or age range so apps can get an age signal. Apps in those stores must ask for that age signal when first opened or when an account is made, and providers must share only the minimum needed information. The law also sets civil fines of up to $2,500 per minor for each negligent violation and up to $7,500 per minor for each intentional violation, and it applies to covered apps and device users.

CO-2026A-SB6.s: The law requires health insurance plans that cover prescription drugs to treat non-opioid pain drugs no more strictly than opioid pain drugs. It also says the out-of-pocket cost for a non-opioid pain drug cannot be higher than for an opioid pain drug, and some plans must have at least one non-opioid option available when it is a good medical fit. The new rules start for individual and small group plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2027, and for large employer plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2028; it also includes a $15,415 state cost to help carry out the law.
